source: From Harm to Help: Turning Reasoning In-Context Demos into Assets for Reasoning LMs (arXiv 2509.23196, Sep 2025)
finding: Adding one or three retrieved reasoning demonstrations (full worked solutions with CoT) to the prompt of reasoning models lowers accuracy below direct zero-shot answering. Harm is larger on hard competition math than on science QA, and grows with more demos.
numbers: Text estimates (main effect shown only in Figure 1): AIME 2025, 1 demo: drop of about 6 to 16 points; 3 demos: drop up to 35 points. GPQA Diamond: 1 demo 1 to 5 points; 3 demos 4 to 8 points. Models in the motivation section: Qwen3 1.5B/3B/8B and R1-Distill 7B/32B. Only k=1 and k=3 tested (no k=2, 4).
limits: Exact per-model drops are only in plots. Model lists differ between motivation and main sections. Demos are retrieved full CoT traces, not curated worked examples. No human-style problem-vs-example control at matched tokens.
agent_relevance: Closes the main part of gap 1: for o1/R1-class models, raw stored solutions in context hurt, and a 6,000-token trace is a large load. A subgoal library should store short distilled insights, not full traces.

source: From Harm to Help (arXiv 2509.23196), Tables 1-3 and token table
finding: Converting the same demonstrations into short reusable insights (I2S, I2S+) fixes the harm and beats direct answering. A full reasoning demo averages about 6,142 tokens on AIME25, far larger than the question.
numbers: Direct vs I2S+ accuracy: AIME25 R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 42.00 to 51.33; 14B 50.00 to 60.00; Qwen3-1.7B 35.96 to 42.65. GPQA 7B 51.26 to 55.16; 14B 59.50 to 63.03. Text: GPT-4.1 on AIME 34.0 to 48.0 (+14.0); o1-mini +2.7 AIME, +1.7 GPQA. Token table (AIME25 avg): demo question 111.6, demo CoT 6141.8, demo answer 751.2, target question 154.5. General Reasoning sets: gains mixed, some variants below Direct.
limits: Text figures and Table 1 disagree for R1-Distill-7B (text +12.0/+4.8, table +9.33/+3.90). Table header says Maj@3, text says maj@33. Compute match is approximate.
agent_relevance: The fix is the same idea as fading or schema abstraction: keep the principle, drop the long trace. Supports storing compact subgoal notes over whole solutions for reasoning-class models.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Prompting: Zero-shot Can Be Stronger than Few-shot (EMNLP Findings; arXiv 2506.14641)
finding: For strong instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5 family), 8-shot CoT exemplars do not beat zero-shot CoT on math once evaluation is fixed. Exemplars mostly align output format. Enhanced exemplars written by Qwen2.5-Max or DeepSeek-R1 also do not help. Attention to the exemplar section is low.
numbers: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct: GSM8K 8-shot 95.75, zero-shot 91.58 (script bug), zero-shot-fixed 95.83; MATH 8-shot 81.30, zero-shot 81.64. Base 72B: GSM8K 90.52 vs 84.69 (fixed 90.27); MATH 75.82 vs 70.60. Retrieval selectors (TopK, MMR, DPP, EXPLORA and others, 8 shots) gain at most about 0.2 points. Non-math: LSAT-LR 72B 41.55 few vs 84.65 zero; CommonsenseQA 7B 25.14 vs 79.85.
limits: Main curves are in figures with no numbers in the text. The non-math few-shot collapse looks partly like a format failure. Instruction-tuned models only (one base comparison). Weak models (LLaMA3.2-1B, LLaMA2-7B, Qwen-7B) still gain from exemplars; LLaMA3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-1.5B do not.
agent_relevance: Clearest LLM expertise-reversal analogue: exemplars help weak or base models and format, and stop helping strong instruct models. Do not assume stored examples add reasoning skill for a strong model.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1 (arXiv 2501.12948), limitations and evaluation-prompt sections
finding: The R1 authors state few-shot prompting consistently degrades R1 and recommend a zero-shot prompt that describes the problem and output format. They converted few-shot benchmark prompts to zero-shot for evaluation because few-shot CoT may hurt R1.
numbers: No numbers given. Statements: 'Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance' (limitations); 'The CoT in few-shot may hurt the performance of DeepSeek-R1' (MMLU-Pro, C-Eval, CLUE-WSC converted to zero-shot).
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: Developer claim without ablation data. Confirms the critique: one sentence, no measurement.
agent_relevance: Vendor guidance that agrees with d01 and d03. Treat as direction, not size.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) The Curse of CoT: On the Limitations of Chain-of-Thought in In-Context Learning (arXiv 2504.05081)
finding: On pattern-based in-context learning tasks, direct answering beats CoT and reasoning variants. Long-CoT reasoning models use about 12 times more total tokens and 40 times more inference tokens and are not better than top direct models. The gap widens as demonstrations increase from 3 to 15 on two tasks.
numbers: Across nine datasets, direct beats CoT by 5.10 points absolute (20.42% relative), ReAct by 8.02 (36.34%), ToT by 9.64 (47.17%). Mean accuracy on MiniARC, COGS, RAVEN: Qwen2.5-72B direct 22.52; Gemini-1.5-pro direct 28.38; DeepSeek-V3 direct 26.46; QwQ-32B 13.51; o1-mini 18.68; DeepSeek-R1 26.81 (token cost about 2432 vs about 190 for direct).
limits: Pattern induction, not worked-example transfer. Abstract says 16 models, appendix says 20. No per-shot numbers in the text.
agent_relevance: Learning a rule from examples is a separate weak spot for reasoning models: they infer wrong patterns from demonstrations. A library that relies on analogy from stored cases needs a check step.

source: Tang et al. (2025) The Few-shot Dilemma: Over-prompting Large Language Models (arXiv 2509.13196)
finding: More examples is not always better. In requirement classification, most models peak at about 5 to 20 well-selected examples and then decline, and TF-IDF similarity selection beats random. Some models (DeepSeek-V3, Mistral-7B) keep gaining or plateau.
numbers: 168 runs on binary PROMISE: 7 models x 3 selection methods x 8 example counts (0 to 160). PURE: GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-4B peak at roughly 5 to 20 then decline. Llama-3.2-3B worsens beyond about 80 (original PROMISE). Llama-3.1-8B reaches about 95% weighted F1 with 10 to 20 TF-IDF examples. Binary 10-fold F1: DeepSeek-V3 and Llama-3.1-8B 0.95, GPT-4o 0.93, Llama-3.2-3B 0.48.
limits: Classification, not reasoning or agents. Per-count numbers are in figures only. Peak counts are approximate.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 7: relevance ranking lets small k do the work and extra examples add noise. Favours k about 3 to 6 relevance-ranked subgoal entries, never a whole library.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior (arXiv 2505.16067)
finding: Adding every executed experience to an agent memory (add-all) is worse than a small fixed memory, because errors propagate and agents copy similar past outputs. Adding only experiences that pass a strict check beats both. Solution correctness matters a lot for a stored library.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini. Fixed memory / Add all / Strict add: RegAgent success 67.53 / 55.48 / 70.95; EHRAgent accuracy 16.75 / 13.05 / 38.50; AgentDriver success 40.11 / 32.32 / 51.00; CIC-IoT accuracy 71.50 / 59.90 / 85.40. Coarse GPT-4o-mini judge lands between: EHRAgent 26.19, CIC-IoT 74.00.
limits: Memory of past task input-output records, not subgoal solutions. The strict check uses ground-truth or strong evaluator signals not always available. Single backbone for main results.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 for the direction: verified entries help, unverified self-generated entries can be worse than none. Gate the subgoal library on a real verifier.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) memory management study, deletion experiments and quality tables (arXiv 2505.16067)
finding: Deleting stored records helps when the add rule was weak and costs little when it was strict. History-based deletion (drop entries whose past use led to poor outcomes) is the most reliable. Periodic deletion shrinks memory a lot at small accuracy cost.
numbers: Strict add, history deletion vs none: EHRAgent 42.06 vs 38.67 (memory 784 vs 1012); CIC-IoT 89.60 vs 85.40; AgentDriver 51.81 vs 51.00; RegAgent 69.80 vs 70.95. Coarse add, history deletion: EHRAgent 33.55 vs 25.91. Retained records were more correct than deleted ones (EHRAgent 4o-mini judge 44.1 vs 36.3; CIC-IoT 78.9 vs 56.7). Combined deletion shrinks EHRAgent strict memory to 248 records.
limits: Differences per task are a few points; no confidence intervals in the text. Table 1 and 2 disagree slightly (38.50 vs 38.67).
agent_relevance: Supports a retire rule for subgoal entries based on later outcomes, linking to the relevance-based memory subfield.

source: Sarukkai et al. (2025) Self-Generated In-Context Examples Improve LLM Agents for Sequential Decision-Making Tasks (arXiv 2505.00234)
finding: An agent that stores its own successful trajectories and retrieves them as examples improves a lot over a fixed hand-written set. Curating the database and the retrieved exemplars adds more. Failed trajectories were not tested; only successes were kept.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini, five seeds. Success Fixed-DB / Traj-Bootstrap / +DB+Exemplar curation: ALFWorld 0.73 / 0.89 / 0.93; InterCode-SQL 0.75 / 0.79 / 0.82; Wordcraft 0.55 / 0.64 / 0.69 (exemplar-only 0.72). Fixed-DB with gpt-4o: ALFWorld 0.88. k = 6 retrieved per step (10 for Wordcraft). Seed examples: 18, 10, 4.
limits: No ablation over k and no unfiltered or failed-trajectory arm visible in the text. Wordcraft text and table disagree (0.71 vs 0.72, 0.67 vs 0.69). Appendix D onward not read.
agent_relevance: Self-generated verified solutions work as worked examples for agents at ordinary k. Gap 6 (unverified entries) and gap 7 (k = 1, 2, 4 sweeps) remain open.

source: Zhao, Yao, Yang, Yu (2024) Large Language Models are In-context Teachers for Knowledge Reasoning (EMNLP Findings; arXiv 2311.06985)
finding: Demonstration rationales work better when they resemble the student model's own self-explanations. A model's own explanations (Self-Explain) beat human-written rationales as demonstrations, and a 7B teacher aligned to GPT-3.5 (Teach-Back) beat human teachers by about 5% in medical QA.
numbers: Medical QA: about 5% higher test accuracy than human teachers, 7B teacher with GPT-3.5 student. Other per-benchmark numbers not read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract page only this session. Explanation is part of the example, not an explain-then-use prompt on a stored solution, so it is not a direct test of gap 5.
agent_relevance: Weak support that stored examples should be written in the agent's own voice. Gap 5 (self-explanation prompts at equal tokens) remains open.

source: Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Clerjuste, Chawla (2023) A Meta-analysis of the Worked Examples Effect on Mathematics Performance (Educational Psychology Review)
finding: The published abstract reports 43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effect sizes from 8,033 screened abstracts, average Hedges g 0.48 (robust variance estimation). The g = 0.43 (40 articles, 49 studies) figure is not in the journal text and is probably an earlier conference version. Self-explanation prompts moderated the effect negatively. Correct examples alone gave larger effects than incorrect or mixed. The effect was medium for both practice and initial skill acquisition.
numbers: g = 0.48, p = 0.01, 43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effect sizes, 8,033 abstracts screened. Moderators: self-explanation prompts (negative), example type (correct alone best), timing (no difference).
quote: pairing examples with self-explanation prompts may not be a fruitful design modification
limits: Abstract only; full text is paywalled. Publication-bias tests (funnel, Egger, trim-and-fill) could not be checked and stay unknown. Mathematics only. Includes grey literature.
agent_relevance: Closes the g discrepancy: use 0.48 with 55 studies. Correct-only beating mixed supports a verified-only library. The negative self-explanation moderator warns against assuming explain-then-use helps.

source: Wittwer and Renkl (2010) How Effective are Instructional Explanations in Example-Based Learning? A Meta-Analytic Review (Educational Psychology Review)
finding: Review of 21 experimental studies. Adding instructional explanations to examples has minimal benefit overall. They help conceptual more than procedural knowledge. They are not more effective than other example-processing supports such as self-explaining.
numbers: 21 experimental studies. Effect sizes not in the abstract.
quote: the benefits of instructional explanations for example-based learning per se are minimal
limits: Abstract only. Not a meta-analysis of the worked-example effect itself. Crissman (2006) dissertation meta-analysis not found this session.
agent_relevance: Extra explanation text attached to a stored solution is not a sure gain. Keep entries short unless the task is conceptual.

source: Salden, Koedinger, Renkl, Aleven, McLaren (2010) Accounting for Beneficial Effects of Worked Examples in Tutored Problem Solving (Educational Psychology Review)
finding: Review of eight studies adding worked examples to Cognitive Tutors (geometry, chemistry, algebra). Examples mostly saved time and did not raise immediate learning, unlike in untutored problem solving. Fading gave better long-term retention in the studies that tested it. Examples never raised time or lowered any outcome.
numbers: Eight studies. Efficiency gain (same learning, less time) in 5 of 8. Conceptual transfer benefit in 1 of 4 that tested it (Schwonke et al. 2009). Long-term retention benefit in 3 of 3 that tested it (Anthony 2008; Salden et al. 2010). Standard tutor students spent 21% (McLaren studies) and 19% (Schwonke studies) more time. About half of the problem steps were replaced by examples. Chemistry studies: 21% less time, equal posttest.
limits: Sample sizes and effect sizes per study are not given in the text read. The tutored control is a strong control, so this bounds the classic effect.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: when the control already scaffolds subgoals (as a scaffolded agent does), stored examples buy efficiency, not accuracy. Measure tokens saved, not just accuracy.

source: Salden, Aleven, Schwonke, Renkl (2010) The expertise reversal effect and worked examples in tutored problem solving (Instructional Science 38; Crossref lists 2009)
finding: One lab and one classroom experiment compared a standard Cognitive Tutor, fixed fading of examples and fading adapted to the student's self-explanation success. Both experiments favoured adaptive fading over fixed fading over problem solving. The review (d13) adds that the gain was on long-term retention, with no transfer difference and no time saving versus the standard tutor.
numbers: Per-group N and effect sizes not available (paywalled). The abstract gives the order: adaptive > fixed > problem solving in both studies. The review reports no significant transfer differences and that fading did not cut instructional time in these two studies.
limits: Abstract plus review description only. The classroom replication is only partial per the earlier critique. Exact Ns remain open (gap 3).
agent_relevance: Only direct human test that fading beats full examples, and only with individually adapted fading. An agent version needs a per-skill competence signal, not a fixed schedule.

source: Schwonke, Renkl, Krieg, Wittwer, Aleven, Salden (2009) The worked-example effect: Not an artefact of lousy control conditions (Computers in Human Behavior 25)
finding: Two geometry Cognitive Tutor studies with fixed fading. Per the Salden 2010 review, tutored problem solving combined with example fading gave at least as much learning and transfer in significantly less instructional time, and the second study found better transfer to conceptually oriented problems.
numbers: Per the review: 19% more time for the standard tutor; conceptual transfer benefit in the second study only. Ns not retrieved (paywalled, Cloudflare block). The task text cites this work as Learning and Instruction; Crossref lists it in Computers in Human Behavior.
limits: Second-hand through d13 and a Semantic Scholar summary; the article itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as d13: strong scaffold plus examples gives efficiency; the transfer gain is not robust.

source: Salden, Aleven, Renkl, Schwonke (2009) Worked Examples and Tutored Problem Solving: Redundant or Synergistic Forms of Support? (Topics in Cognitive Science 1)
finding: Reported (Semantic Scholar summary only) to find that adaptive fading of worked-out examples leads to higher transfer on delayed posttests than fixed fading or tutored problem solving alone.
numbers: Not retrieved. Wiley returned a 403; Ns and effect sizes unknown.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Same as d14. Gap 3 remains open for exact Ns.

source: Sweller and Cooper (1985) The Use of Worked Examples as a Substitute for Problem Solving in Learning Algebra (Cognition and Instruction 2)
finding: Founding study. Not opened: the Taylor and Francis page is blocked and no open copy was found. The 1985 figures from Wikipedia stay unverified.
limits: Both Taylor and Francis and Semantic Scholar show it as closed access.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open for the 1985 numbers; later reviews (d11, d13) cite the effect without changing the claim.

source: Kestin et al. (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT (Scientific Reports; preprint 2024)
finding: A randomized crossover trial in a Harvard physics course found students learned more from an AI tutor than from active learning. The tutor prompts were enriched with comprehensive step-by-step solutions so the LLM could give accurate explanations. It measures test scores, but does not test LLM-generated worked examples against problems.
numbers: 233 enrolled, 194 analysed. Post-test median 4.5 (AI group, n = 142) vs 3.5 (active learning, n = 174); pre-test baseline median 2.75 (n = 316). Effect size 0.63 SD (linear regression), 0.73 to 1.3 SD (quantile regression, ceiling-corrected). Median time on task 49 min in the AI group against an assumed 60 min. 83% said AI explanations were as good as or better than human instructors.
limits: Not a worked-example manipulation. One course, one topic, short sessions. Hand-written solutions supplied to the tutor.
agent_relevance: Partial hit on gap 9: test-score outcome with an LLM given stored step-by-step solutions. It shows solution-in-prompt helps the tutor model, not that learners gain from LLM-made examples.
